Hook: In April 1965 a trade magazine called Electronics asked Gordon Moore, the head of research at Fairchild Semiconductor, what would happen to his industry over the next ten years. He looked at the few chips made so far, each with a handful of components, and noticed that the number on the most economical chip had been doubling every year. 'The complexity for minimum component costs,' he wrote, 'has increased at a rate of roughly a factor of two per year.' Keep doubling for ten years, he said, and by 1975 a single chip would hold 65,000 components. It was a forecast about cost as much as about physics: more on one chip, and each component cheaper.

Twenty-two years later, in 1987, a new company opened in Hsinchu, in Taiwan, with an odd plan. It would make chips, but only other companies' chips. It would design none of its own, so it would not compete with its customers. Anyone with a design could book its factories, as you book a printer. That company is Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, TSMC. In 2025 it made 12,682 different products for 534 customers, and took in about $121 billion.

Moore's doubling and TSMC's factories are the two halves of this story. One made chips ever cheaper to compute with; the other made the factories ever dearer to build, until only a few companies could afford the ones that make the best chips. Industry, Built. Part fifteen: semiconductors. Why do the most advanced chips come from so few factories?
Run: Chapter one. Run it: build a fab or book a foundry.

You run a chip-design company, and your new chip is ready. It is a square of silicon about 100 square millimetres, and each good one sells for $60. You can build your own factory, a fab: about $20 billion, with tools that are obsolete in about 5 years, able to start 50,000 wafers a month. And because the process is new to you, your first wafers will be full of defects. Or you can book a foundry, which already runs the process, at $17,000 a wafer. Which is cheaper depends on one thing: how many wafers you need.

Run it at three sizes. A small company needs five thousand wafers a month. Its own fab would stand 10 per cent full, so each wafer would carry ten times its share of the fab: about $85,833. It would lose about $3.5 billion a year; booking a foundry, it makes about $1.1 billion. At twenty thousand wafers, the fab is 40 per cent full and finally profitable, but still behind the foundry: $2.2 billion against $4.3. Only at fifty thousand, a full fab, does owning win: $13.8 billion against $10.7, because now you keep the foundry's margin yourself.

Draw it for every size. The foundry line rises steadily: you pay per wafer, so profit grows with volume. Your own fab starts deep in loss, because you pay for the whole fab however little you use. They cross at about 32,000 wafers a month, every month, for five years. Very few chip companies need that much of one process. But a foundry adds up everyone's demand: TSMC shipped about 15 million wafers in 2025, more than a million a month, and keeps its fabs full with other people's chips. That arithmetic is why the industry split in two.
Making: Chapter two. How a chip is made.

A chip is built in layers on a polished disc of silicon, a wafer, by repeating one loop over and over. Lay down a thin film of material. Coat it with a light-sensitive resist. Shine light through a mask, the pattern for that layer, focused down by a lens onto the wafer. Wash away the resist the light has touched. Etch the film wherever it is now bare. Strip off the rest of the resist, clean, and start again with the next layer: transistors at the bottom, then layer upon layer of wiring to join them.

The smallest thing you can print is set by the light. Smaller features need shorter wavelengths. ASML's lamps and lasers give light of 365, 248 and 193 nanometres, all still in use. The most advanced machines now use extreme ultraviolet light, 13.5 nanometres. The rule the toolmakers work by: the smallest feature is a constant times the wavelength, divided by the lens's numerical aperture. Over forty years, ASML says, that has improved a hundredfold. And only one company in the world makes the machines that use extreme ultraviolet light: ASML, in the Netherlands.

After many turns of the loop, the wafer holds a grid of identical chips. A wafer 300 millimetres across holds about 640 dies of a hundred square millimetres. Each is tested on the wafer, and the failures marked. The good ones are cut out, mounted in a package that connects them to the outside world, and tested again. In 1961 the lines on a chip were about 25 micrometres wide; in 1975, about 5, Moore reported. In 2026 TSMC was selling chips made on a process it calls two nanometres.
Node: Every few years the industry moves to a new 'node', a new generation of process. When Moore wrote, the number was a real measurement: lines 25 micrometres wide in 1961, 5 by 1975. Today's numbers, TSMC's three and two nanometres, are the names each company gives its generations. Intel calls its newest one 18A, A for angstrom, a tenth of a nanometre. What each new generation actually delivers is more transistors in the same space, using less power, and the new transistor shapes that make that possible: Intel's 18A brought transistors wrapped in their gate on every side, and power wired in from the back of the wafer.

Why chase the next node? Because that is where the money goes. Here is TSMC's wafer revenue by node. In 2023, its three-nanometre process brought in 6 per cent. In 2024, 18. In 2025, 24. And in the third quarter of 2026, 33 per cent, with the two-nanometre process already at 8. Each new node takes over the top of the market within a few years, at the highest prices, because the customers who need the fastest chips will pay for them. The older nodes do not disappear; they become the factories for everything else.
Yield: Every wafer comes out of the fab with a few specks of dust or flaws scattered across it, and a die with a flaw in the wrong place is scrap. Take two wafers with the same scattering of defects. One is cut into small dies, a hundred square millimetres each; the other into big ones, eight hundred. Here are the defects. On the small dies, a defect ruins one small die: about 90 per cent come out good. On the big dies, the same defects ruin far more silicon: only about 45 per cent are good. A big die costs more than its area, because each flaw throws away more.

If defects fall at random, the share of good dies falls exponentially with the die's area times the defect density. On a mature process, with one defect in ten square centimetres, small chips nearly all work and big ones mostly do. On a new process, with three or five defects per ten square centimetres, small chips still come out well, but big ones are mostly scrap. So on a new process the small chips pay first, and the biggest chips are worth making only once the process has matured.

Defect density is not fixed. Every wafer a fab makes on a process teaches its engineers something, and the defects fall: fast at first, then slowly. So the first company to reach a new node gets down the curve first, and can sell its customers good chips while rivals are still scrapping theirs. TSMC's gross margin went from 54.4 per cent in 2023 to 59.9 in 2025, which it put down to fuller fabs and lower costs, and to 66.4 in the third quarter of 2026.
Fab: A fab is a building full of machines, and TSMC writes its machines off over 5 years, so a chipmaker never stops buying them. Here is TSMC's revenue, year by year. And here is what it spent on fabs and tools: between 31 and 53 per cent of its revenue, every year. In 2025 that came to about $41 billion; for 2026 it planned 52 to 56 billion. And it has said it expects to invest $165 billion in America alone: six fabs, two packaging plants and a research centre.

Because the fab costs the same whether it is busy or idle, how full it is decides everything. In the Works' fab, a wafer costs about $86 thousand to make when the fab runs at a tenth of its capacity, and about $11 thousand when it is full. TSMC had capacity for more than 17 million wafers in 2025 and shipped about 15 million: about 88 per cent full. And it earned more for each one: about NT$180 thousand a wafer in 2023, NT$254 thousand in 2025, about $8,100, as more of its wafers were on its newest processes. Its margin rose, it said, mainly because of higher utilization and lower costs.

And the people. At the end of 2023 TSMC employed about 76,478 people. By the end of 2025, about 90,557. That is about $1.3 million of revenue for each of them. A fab is a building full of machines, and the money goes on the machines: as we saw, a third to a half of TSMC's revenue every year. Very few industries take in so much for each person they employ.
Split: The Run it chapter's arithmetic split the industry in two. On one side, designers with no factories at all, called fabless: Nvidia, Broadcom, Qualcomm, AMD. They send their designs to foundries, which make chips for anyone. Both depend on the toolmakers and the design-software companies. On the other side, the integrated makers who still design and make their own: Intel, Texas Instruments, Micron. Nvidia says in its annual report that it uses foundries such as TSMC and Samsung.

And the foundry's customers are concentrated. TSMC does not name them, but its largest customer brought in 19 per cent of its revenue in 2025, the second 17 per cent, and the ten largest together 78 per cent, up from 70 per cent two years earlier. The foundry is shared by hundreds of companies, but paid for by a few.

The fabless model's biggest winner is Nvidia. Its revenue was about $7 billion in fiscal 2017. In the year to January 2026 it was about $216 billion, with about $120 billion of profit, $194 billion of it from chips for data centres, up from $48 billion two years before. It owns no fab. Every one of those chips was made by a foundry.

The other way, making chips for yourself and others, is the hardest. Intel has tried to become a foundry too. Its foundry division lost about $7 billion in 2023, $13 billion in 2024 and $10 billion in 2025. Of its $18 billion of revenue in 2025, only about $307 million came from outside customers; the rest was Intel's own chips. Intel says that without a significant outside customer it may pause its next process altogether. In August 2025 the US government took 275 million Intel shares, in a deal that released the subsidies it had already promised. A fab needs volume, and volume is exactly what the foundry model gives TSMC and denies its rivals.
Tools: A fab's machines come from specialist makers, and at the very front there is only one. ASML, a Dutch company, sold €32.7 billion of machines and service in 2025. It sold 327 lithography systems, 48 of them the extreme-ultraviolet machines that print the finest layers of the newest chips. It is, in its own words, the world's only manufacturer of them, and their optics come from one supplier, Carl Zeiss. One maker of the machine the newest chips need: which is why, as we will see, governments decide who may buy one.

Behind ASML stand a few more specialists. Applied Materials, Lam Research and KLA make many of the other machines: the ones that lay down films, etch them away, and inspect the wafer for flaws. And Synopsys and Cadence sell the software that chip designers use to draw billions of transistors and check that they will work. Every one of them kept at least 19 per cent of its revenue as profit in its latest year. In a gold rush, the shovel makers do well whoever strikes gold.

Now follow the money upstream, from the chip to the machines. In the year to January 2026 Nvidia sold $216 billion of chips and systems, and kept 71 dollars of every hundred as gross profit. The rest, about $62 billion, paid for making them: wafers from its foundries, TSMC and Samsung; memory from SK hynix, Micron and Samsung; packaging; and assembly by contract manufacturers. Upstream, TSMC took in $121 billion in 2025 from all its customers, its largest alone bringing in 19 per cent. It spent $41 billion on fabs and tools, money that flows on to the toolmakers: Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA and ASML. At every step the stream is smaller, and at every step a company with few rivals keeps a large share of it.
Intermission: An intermission, and two lines from America's official statistics. The Federal Reserve's index of American output of semiconductors and other electronic components: about 5,089 times as much in 2025 as in 1972. And the government's producer price index for semiconductors, after allowing for inflation: down about 98 per cent since 1967. In money that is not adjusted for inflation it fell by 81 per cent, while prices in general rose about 10 times.

And here is Moore's law itself. The number of transistors on a microprocessor, from about 2,308 in 1971 to about 58 billion in 2021. In 1975 Moore had revised his forecast to a doubling every two years. Over the next half-century the counts doubled about every 2.0 years. The forecast held for half a century, because an industry spent ever more money to keep it true.
Memory: Memory chips are different. One maker's memory does much the same job as another's, so they sell close to a commodity, at whatever the market pays. Here is Micron, America's memory maker, quarter by quarter since 2008. In the bad years it loses money: in early 2023 it lost about $2.3 billion in a single quarter. And then this: in the quarter to September 2026, $54 billion of revenue, and $44 billion of operating profit, eight dollars in every ten. The same factories, the same kind of product: only the price changed.

Across the whole industry: the world bought about $130 billion of memory chips in 2022, and about $92 billion in 2023, when prices collapsed. Then $166 billion, and $230 billion in 2025. For 2026 the industry's own statisticians forecast more than $804 billion, three and a half times as much, driven, they said, by AI infrastructure and the high-bandwidth memory that feeds AI chips. In the first half of 2026 memory sales were up 305 per cent. If every maker builds new factories in a boom like this, the factories open together, and that is how a famine starts: the cycle of Part six.

And through the swings, the spending does not stop. Here is what Micron spent on fabs and tools, year by year. In the bust of fiscal 2023 its revenue fell to about $16 billion, and it still spent about $7.7 billion, 49 cents of every dollar it took in: a memory maker that stops shrinking its cells falls behind. In fiscal 2026, with prices soaring, it spent about $31 billion. That capacity will arrive whatever prices are by then, which is how a memory boom plants the seeds of the next bust.
Trailing: Chapter nine. Analog, power and the trailing edge.

Most chips are not at the frontier at all. The chips that manage power, read sensors and convert signals are made on older, cheaper processes, and sold for years. A car is full of them. In 2021, when they ran short, General Motors told its shareholders that the chip shortage cost it more production than the pandemic shutdowns of 2020 had. Even at TSMC, about 19 per cent of wafer revenue in 2025 still came from processes of 28 nanometres and older: fabs whose machines were written off long ago, making chips that do not need to be the smallest.

These are the companies that make them. Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, NXP, Microchip, onsemi and STMicroelectronics. Through the shortage years their margins swelled; Texas Instruments kept 44 cents in the dollar at the peak. Then demand from the carmakers and factories that buy their chips weakened, and by 2025 three of the six were keeping almost nothing. These are steady businesses compared with memory, but they have a cycle of their own, and it follows cars and factories, not AI.
Markets: Chapter ten. Where the chips go.

Where do all these chips go? Start with what they are. In 2025 the world bought about $796 billion of semiconductors, by the count of WSTS, the industry's own statisticians. The biggest slice, about $300 billion, was logic: chips that compute, from the accelerators in AI servers to the chips that run networks. Next came memory, about $230 billion: the business of booms and busts we met in chapter eight. Then three slices of about $85 to $95 billion each: the analog chips that handle power and signals, the microprocessors and microcontrollers, and a mixed bag of single transistors, light-emitting chips and sensors.

And who buys them? TSMC reports its revenue by the kind of product its chips end up in. In 2023, high-performance computing, its name for the processors and accelerators in computers and servers, brought in 43 per cent, and smartphones 38 per cent. Then computing pulled ahead: 51 per cent in 2024, 58 in 2025. In the third quarter of 2026, 68 per cent, against 21 for smartphones. In 2025 computing alone brought TSMC about NT$2.2 trillion, 2.3 times as much as two years before. Cars, for all the trouble of the shortage, were about 5 per cent. The phone built the modern chip industry; computing now pays most of its bills.

One more split, and it explains this year. In 2025 the world bought about $796 billion of chips, $230 billion of it memory. For 2026, WSTS's forecast of May was about $1,511 billion, with memory at $804 billion. Of the forecast increase of $716 billion, about $574 billion, 80 per cent, is memory. The boom of 2026 is, more than anything, a boom in the price of memory, the most cyclical chip of all.
Geography: Chapter eleven. Geography and the state.

Where are the chips made? Take the biggest foundry. TSMC listed 16 fabs in operation in early 2026. 11 of them are in Taiwan, in three science parks: Hsinchu, Central Taiwan and Southern Taiwan. And the 3 fabs making its most advanced chips, at two and three nanometres, are all among them. The rest are abroad: an old fab in Washington State, two in China, one in Kumamoto in Japan, and in Arizona a fab producing since 2024 at 5 nanometres. A fab in Dresden, Germany, is being built. The most valuable machines in the industry sit, for now, mostly on one island.

Governments want those fabs at home, and they pay for them. In November 2024 America's Commerce Department agreed to give TSMC's Arizona company up to $6.6 billion under the CHIPS Act, and to lend it up to 5 billion more. A month later Germany agreed to up to 5 billion euros of state aid for TSMC's fab in Dresden. And, as we saw, the American government now holds 275 million shares of Intel. A chip factory used to be a business decision. Now it is also a matter of state.

And governments decide who may buy the chips. In October 2022 America required licences to send China the most advanced AI chips and the tools to make them. It tightened the rules in October 2023, and in December 2024 extended them to more chipmaking machines made abroad with American technology. In January 2025 it published a framework to ration AI chips across the whole world. It was never enforced. In April 2025 even Nvidia's H20, a chip it sold in China, needed a licence, and Nvidia took a charge of $4.5 billion. Then the rules loosened: licences for some H20s that August, and in January 2026 case-by-case review for the more powerful H200. And in November 2026 a new rule reached data centres abroad that rent computing to Chinese companies, required licences for five more countries, and formally rescinded the 2025 framework. For a chip company, who may buy is now a forecast in itself.

And where are chips bought? WSTS also counts sales by where the buyer is. In 2025 buyers in Asia Pacific took the most, about $440 billion, then the Americas, $256 billion, Europe $55 billion, and Japan $45 billion. For 2026, its spring forecast had sales to the Americas up 112 per cent, to $544 billion, the fastest growth of any region, against 58 per cent for Europe and 28 for Japan. The chips are made mostly in Asia, and bought, more and more, wherever the data centres are being built.
Landscape: The landscape, as of November 2026, for the chip companies that file accounts in America. Across: revenue in the latest year. Up: profit kept per dollar, averaged over five years. The foundries: TSMC, with about $121 billion of revenue and about 41 cents kept in every dollar, far above GlobalFoundries and UMC. The fabless designers: Nvidia, the biggest of all, with about 43 cents; Broadcom and Qualcomm behind it; AMD and Marvell kept much less. Micron, the memory maker: $133 billion in its latest year, but only about 16 cents on average across the cycle. The integrated makers: Intel, $53 billion of revenue and about one cent kept on average; the analog makers, smaller and steadier. And the toolmakers, design-software companies and Amkor, the packager. Beyond the chart, with no American filings: Samsung and SK hynix in Korea, SMIC in China, MediaTek in Taiwan, Tokyo Electron in Japan, Infineon in Germany.

What to watch. Memory prices, and when the boom turns, as memory booms always have. TSMC's spending: 52 to 56 billion dollars planned for 2026, as its two-nanometre fabs fill. Intel's next process, which it says it may pause without an outside customer. The rules on who may buy, and now who may rent, the newest chips. The trailing edge: when cars and factories buy again. And the size of the whole market this year, which brings us to our call.
Called: Two forecasts about chips, one old and one new. In April 1965 Gordon Moore, then at Fairchild, wrote that the number of components on the cheapest chip to make had been doubling every year, and that by 1975 it would be 65,000: ten more doublings. In 1975 he checked. A 16,384-bit memory chip of that year sat where the line said it would. Then he slowed the forecast to a doubling every two years, the version that, as the intermission showed, held for the next half-century.

The new forecast is the industry's own. In December 2025, WSTS, the statistics body the chipmakers run together, forecast that 2026 would approach a trillion dollars: $975 billion, up about a quarter on 2025. By June the first half alone had brought in $702 billion. Add the third quarter, about $518 billion, and by September the year had passed $1.2 trillion, with a quarter still to go. WSTS raised its forecast to $1.51 trillion in May, and to $1.66 trillion in August. The miss was memory: forecast in December at $295 billion for 2026, and in May at $804 billion. Called it? No. Even the industry's own statisticians did not see the size of this boom coming.

Now our own call, written down so you can check it. To pass $1.8 trillion for the year, the fourth quarter has to bring in about $580 billion: 12 per cent more than the third. Sales have grown by more than a fifth a quarter for three quarters running, so we think it will. Against us: memory booms end abruptly, as chapter eight showed, and buyers who stocked up early can stop ordering all at once. We give it 65 per cent, and we will check it against WSTS's first full-year figure, due early in 2027, right or wrong.
Outro: So: why do the most advanced chips come from so few factories? Demand is wide: TSMC alone made 12,682 products for 534 customers in 2025. But Moore's doubling had a price. Each step down in size needs a dearer factory, and only a company with enough customers can fill one: TSMC spent about $41 billion on its fabs in that one year. At the frontier, the 3 fabs that make its two- and three-nanometre chips are all in Taiwan. And the machines that print the finest layers come from one company in the Netherlands. The funnel narrows at every step, because every step costs more than the last, and each one needs the volume of the whole world to pay for it.

Semiconductors, in five answers. What is sold is a die cut from a wafer, more and more often designed by one company and made by another. It is made in hundreds of steps, in factories that cost tens of billions. The dollar goes to the designer with the best chip, to the foundry that can make it, and to the makers of the tools. It stays there because the frontier needs the volume of the whole world, and few can afford to buy in. And what moves it is the memory cycle, the next node, the appetite of AI, and the rules on who may buy. Next time: electronics, the industry that puts these chips into the things we buy, and why the company that builds the device keeps the least of it.
